name: Mochi Ice Cream
instructions: Mix mochiko, sugar, and water until smooth.
Microwave 1 minute, stir, repeat 2 more times.
Knead dough on cornstarch-dusted surface.
Scoop ice cream into balls, freeze solid.
Wrap each ball with mochi dough, seal edges.
tips: Work quickly — mochi gets sticky as it cools.

name: Matcha Soft Serve
instructions: Whisk matcha with a little hot water to make a smooth paste.
Heat milk and sugar until dissolved, cool completely.
Mix cream, milk mixture, matcha paste, and vanilla.
Churn in ice cream maker until soft-serve consistency.
Serve immediately or freeze for firmer texture.
tips: Sift the matcha well to avoid bitterness and lumps.

name: Dorayaki (Red Bean Pancakes)
instructions: Whisk eggs, sugar, and honey until pale.
Sift in flour and mix into a smooth batter. Rest 15 minutes.
Cook small pancakes on a low-heat non-stick pan until golden.
Sandwich a generous amount of anko between two pancakes.
Serve at room temperature.
tips: These are Doraemon’s favorite snack — classic Japanese comfort dessert.

name: Mitarashi Dango
instructions: Mix flour and water into a soft dough, roll into small balls.
Boil until they float, then transfer to cold water.
Skewer 3–4 dumplings per stick.
Make a sweet-savory glaze with soy, sugar, mirin, and starch.
Brush or pour the glaze over the dango and serve.
tips: The glaze should be sticky and glossy — the signature of mitarashi.

name: Warabi Mochi
instructions: Mix warabi mochiko, sugar, and water in a saucepan.
Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly until thick and translucent.
Pour into a wet mold or tray and cool completely (or chill).
Cut into bite-sized pieces and coat with kinako.
Serve with kuromitsu syrup.
tips: A jiggly, cooling summer dessert. Kinako prevents sticking and adds nutty flavor.

name: Anmitsu
instructions: Make agar jelly according to package, cool, and cut into cubes.
Arrange jelly cubes, fruit, and anko in a bowl.
Add soft mochi or shiratama if using.
Pour kuromitsu (or matcha syrup) over the top.
Serve chilled.
tips: A classic Japanese parfait-style dessert — colorful, light, and not too sweet.

name: Tangyuan (Sweet Glutinous Rice Balls)
instructions: Mix flour and water into a smooth dough, rest 20 minutes.
Divide dough, flatten, fill with black sesame paste, seal into balls.
Boil water with ginger and sugar for syrup.
Cook tangyuan until they float (about 5–7 minutes).
Serve in the sweet ginger syrup.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so it doesn’t dry out.

name: Mango Pudding
instructions: Blend mango flesh until smooth.
Bloom gelatin in water, then dissolve over low heat with sugar.
Mix gelatin mixture into mango puree and evaporated milk.
Pour into molds and refrigerate until set (at least 3 hours).
Serve chilled, optionally with extra mango cubes.
tips: Hong Kong-style mango pudding is silky and not overly sweet.

name: Red Bean Soup (Hong Dou Tang)

ingredients.name: Optional: glutinous rice balls or lotus seeds

instructions: Soak red beans for a few hours or overnight.
Boil with plenty of water and optional tangerine peel until very soft.
Mash some of the beans for a thicker texture if desired.
Add sugar and simmer until dissolved.
Serve hot in winter or chilled in summer.
tips: A classic Chinese dessert soup — simple, wholesome, and comforting.

name: Almond Tofu (Xingren Doufu)
instructions: Bloom agar-agar or gelatin in a little water.
Heat remaining liquid with sugar until dissolved, then add the setting agent.
Stir in almond extract (or use almond milk as base).
Pour into a dish and chill until firm.
Cut into cubes and serve with fruit syrup or fresh fruit.
tips: Light, fragrant, and cooling — a classic dim-sum and home dessert.

name: Tanghulu (Candied Fruit Skewers)
instructions: Wash and thoroughly dry the fruit, then skewer them.
Cook sugar and water over medium heat until it reaches hard-crack stage (about 150°C).
Quickly dip or pour the hot syrup over the fruit to coat.
Place on a greased surface or parchment to harden.
Serve once the candy shell is completely set and crunchy.
tips: Work fast — the sugar hardens quickly. Classic winter street snack in northern China.

name: Black Sesame Soup
instructions: Toast black sesame seeds until fragrant, then grind finely.
Mix ground sesame with a little rice flour and water to form a paste.
Bring remaining water to a boil, whisk in the sesame paste.
Simmer until slightly thickened, sweeten to taste.
Serve hot, optionally with a splash of milk.
tips: Nutty, toasty, and warming — a classic Chinese dessert soup especially popular in cooler weather.

name: Bingsu (Shaved Ice)
instructions: Shave frozen milk into fine, fluffy ice.
Top with red beans, fruits, and mochi.
Drizzle generously with condensed milk.
Serve immediately and mix as you eat.
tips: Use a good shaved-ice machine for the fluffiest texture. Classic summer dessert.

name: Yakgwa (Honey Cookies)
instructions: Mix flour with sesame oil and soju into a dough.
Roll out and cut into flower or diamond shapes.
Deep-fry slowly on low heat until golden and cooked through.
Soak the fried cookies in warm honey-ginger syrup.
Drain and top with pine nuts.
tips: These traditional Korean sweets keep well and are often served during holidays.

name: Injeolmi (Soybean Powder Rice Cakes)
instructions: Mix glutinous rice flour with salt and water into a soft dough.
Steam the dough until cooked and sticky (about 25–30 minutes).
Pound or knead the hot rice cake until elastic.
Cut into bite-sized pieces and coat thoroughly with soybean powder mixed with sugar.
Serve at room temperature.
tips: Chewy, nutty, and mildly sweet — a classic Korean rice cake dessert.

name: Sujeonggwa (Cinnamon Punch)
instructions: Simmer cinnamon sticks and ginger in plenty of water for 30–40 minutes.
Strain, then sweeten the liquid with sugar or honey.
Cool completely and chill.
Serve in bowls with a dried persimmon and a few pine nuts floating on top.
tips: A traditional Korean dessert drink — fragrant, spicy-sweet, and usually served cold after a meal.

name: Gyeongdan (Sweet Rice Balls)

ingredients.name: Sweet red bean or sesame filling
Various coatings (soybean powder, black sesame, mugwort)

instructions: Mix glutinous rice flour with hot water into a soft dough.
Divide, flatten, fill with red bean or sesame paste, and seal into balls.
Boil until they float, then cool briefly.
Roll each ball in different coatings for color and flavor variety.
Serve at room temperature.
tips: Often made for celebrations — the colorful coatings make them look festive.

name: Dasik (Traditional Pressed Sweets)

ingredients.name: Roasted soybean powder or green tea powder or black sesame
Optional: pine nuts or flower petals

instructions: Mix the powder with honey or rice syrup until it holds together when pressed.
Press firmly into a dasik mold (or shape into small discs by hand).
Gently release and arrange on a plate.
Optional: decorate with a pine nut or petal.
Serve with tea.
tips: These delicate traditional Korean sweets are often served during ceremonies or with tea. Very little effort, elegant result.

name: Halo-Halo

ingredients.name: Sweetened red beans + nata de coco + macapuno

instructions: Layer sweetened beans, fruits, and jellies in a tall glass.
Add shaved ice to fill the glass.
Top with leche flan and a scoop of ube ice cream.
Pour evaporated milk over everything.
Mix thoroughly before eating.
tips: Mix everything together for the full halo-halo experience.

name: Leche Flan
instructions: Melt sugar in a pan until golden caramel, pour into mold.
Gently mix yolks, both milks, and vanilla (do not overbeat).
Strain mixture into caramel-lined mold.
Steam 40–45 minutes or bake in water bath until set.
Cool completely, then invert onto plate.
tips: Strain the custard twice for the silkiest texture.

name: Ube Halaya (Purple Yam Jam)
instructions: Cook grated ube with coconut milk over medium heat, stirring constantly.
Add condensed milk, butter, and sugar.
Keep stirring until the mixture becomes very thick and glossy.
Transfer to a greased dish and smooth the top.
Cool completely before serving.
tips: Continuous stirring is necessary so it doesn’t stick or burn.

name: Buko Pandan
instructions: Prepare pandan gelatin according to package, cool, and cube.
Mix buko strips, gelatin cubes, and kaong if using.
Fold in condensed milk and cream (or all-purpose cream).
Chill for at least 1 hour.
Serve cold.
tips: A light, fragrant Filipino dessert that’s perfect after a heavy meal.

name: Bibingka
instructions: Mix rice flour, coconut milk, eggs, sugar, and baking powder into a batter.
Line molds with banana leaves and pour in the batter.
Top with slices of salted egg and grated cheese.
Bake or cook in a special bibingka oven until set and lightly browned.
Brush with butter and sprinkle with more coconut or sugar if desired.
tips: Traditionally cooked with heat from both top and bottom. The banana leaf adds aroma.

name: Mais con Yelo
instructions: Place sweet corn in the bottom of serving glasses or bowls.
Pile shaved ice on top.
Drizzle generously with condensed milk and evaporated milk.
Add a little sugar if desired.
Mix and eat immediately.
tips: A simple, nostalgic Filipino merienda dessert — sweet corn and cold milk over ice.

name: Thai Coconut Ice Cream (I-Tim Kati)
instructions: Mix coconut milk, condensed milk, sugar, and salt.
Optional: heat with cornstarch to thicken, then cool.
Churn in ice cream maker or freeze, stirring every 30 minutes.
Serve in small cups or on a stick with toppings (peanuts, sticky rice).
tips: Street-style version is often served with roasted peanuts and sticky rice.

name: Khanom Buang (Thai Crispy Pancakes)

ingredients.name: Egg yolks (foi thong style) or meringue

instructions: Make a thin batter and cook small crispy crepes on a hot pan.
Spread a layer of sweet coconut cream on each.
Top with golden egg yolk threads or fluffy meringue.
Fold or leave open and serve.
Best eaten fresh while still crispy.
tips: These are a popular Thai street dessert — crispy outside, creamy inside.

name: Tub Tim Grob (Red Rubies in Coconut Milk)
instructions: Color the water chestnut pieces red and coat them in tapioca flour.
Boil until they float and look like little jewels, then cool in ice water.
Make sweetened coconut milk with a pinch of salt.
Place the red rubies in bowls, add coconut milk and crushed ice.
Serve immediately.
tips: The chewy ‘rubies’ in icy coconut milk are a classic Thai dessert.

name: Kluay Buat Chee (Banana in Coconut Milk)
instructions: Peel and cut bananas into chunks.
Gently simmer coconut milk with sugar, salt, and pandan until the sugar dissolves.
Add banana pieces and cook until just tender (don’t overcook or they fall apart).
Serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: A simple, comforting Thai dessert — the bananas should stay intact and slightly firm.

name: Lod Chong (Pandan Noodles in Coconut Milk)
instructions: Make a green dough with flours and pandan juice, cook until thick.
Press the dough through a sieve or mold into boiling water to form short noodles.
Cool the noodles in ice water.
Make sweetened, slightly salty coconut milk.
Serve noodles in bowls with coconut milk and crushed ice.
tips: The bright green pandan noodles in cold coconut milk are a classic Thai refresher.

name: Sankaya Fak Thong (Pumpkin Custard)
instructions: Cut the top off the pumpkin and clean out the seeds.
Whisk eggs, coconut milk, sugar, salt, and pandan until smooth.
Pour the custard into the pumpkin shell.
Steam gently for 40–50 minutes until the custard is set.
Cool slightly, then slice into wedges and serve.
tips: The pumpkin becomes the edible bowl — beautiful presentation and delicious contrast of textures.
